Text Reminders and FIT Kit Returns

A Three-Window Bayesian Hierarchical Model: Design, Changes and Results

[Author names]

November 15, 2026

Key Findings

  • Reminders increased returns. Among kits dispensed in 2022–2023, the model estimates a return rate of 83.7% with the text-reminder program, versus 76.5% had the same kits received no reminders. That is an increase of 7.2 points (95% CrI 4.5 to 10.1). The posterior probability that reminders helped at all is >99%; the probability that the gain exceeds 5 points is 95%.
  • The gain appears only after reminders started. The share of kits returned in the first 14 days, before any reminder, was 43.9% before 2022 and 43.0% after. Among kits still out at day 14, the share returned during days 15–90 (the reminder period) rose from 53.7% to 63.0%. Among kits still out at day 90, very late returns also rose, from 13.5% to 22.6%.
  • Placebo check. Patients who declined texts, and so should not have been reminded, had an estimated gain of 0.7 points (95% CrI -5.0 to 6.4), versus 7.6 points (95% CrI 4.8 to 10.4) for patients who consented. The probability that consenters gained more is 99%.
  • Subgroups. The gain was 8.2 points for women and 6.0 for men (probability women gained more: 98%). The reminder effect changed by 0.20 (95% CrI -0.01 to 0.43) log-odds per decade of age (probability it grows with age: 97%). Other subgroup differences were small and uncertain.

1 Why a New Model

The original analysis (OMED 2025 poster) used a Bayesian hierarchical binomial model. Peer review raised concerns that this model did not resolve:

  1. Repeated kits from the same patient. 78% of kits come from patients who received more than one kit. These kits are not independent: patients tend to return all of their kits or none. The original model had random effects for demographic groups, but no patient-level effect, so it did not account for this.
  2. Differences between the pre and post cohorts in age, prior screening and language.
  3. Inconsistent numbers between the poster and the manuscript.
  4. Exposure: not every post-period kit received a reminder. Texts were sent only to kits not yet returned, every two weeks from day 14 to day 90.
  5. Subgroup conclusions (age, sex, language) made without analyses that directly test them.

The new model addresses each of these. The changes are listed in Changes from the Original Model.

2 Data

The analysis uses 4,302 FIT kits dispensed to 2,092 patients between January 2019 and December 2023: 1,742 before reminders began (2019–2021) and 2,560 after (2022–2023). Data cleaning is documented separately (audit log and EDA report).

Outcome. A kit counts as returned if it was returned at any point before data extraction. The latest return in the file is June 05, 2024, so every kit had at least five months of follow-up.

Kits per patient (requested by the reviewer):

3 The Model

3.1 Three-Window Design

In the post period, a text reminder was sent every two weeks from day 14 to day 90 after a kit was dispensed. Texts stopped as soon as the kit was returned, and stopped for good at day 90. A reminder can therefore only have influenced a kit that was still out at day 14, and mainly during days 15–90. The model follows each kit through three windows:

  • Window 1 (days 0–14): was the kit returned by day 14? No kit, before or after 2022, had received a reminder yet. Any change here after 2022 reflects other changes over time.
  • Window 2 (days 15–90): for kits still out at day 14, was the kit returned by day 90? This is where reminders operate in the post period.
  • Window 3 (after day 90): for kits still out at day 90, was the kit ever returned? Reminders had stopped. A separate term captures any post-period difference here: late responses to the final texts, or a different mix of kits still outstanding.

Reminders work only in window 2. Most non-reminder changes (staffing, kit type, patient mix) would affect every window. Comparing the post-2022 change in window 2 with the change in window 1 therefore separates the reminder effect from everything else that changed in 2022, like a control group built into the timeline.

Key assumption. Without reminders, changes after 2022 would have shifted returns in each window by the same amount on the odds scale. The pre-period placebo test (see Limitations and Next Steps) is designed to check this.

3.2 Model Components

Component What it does Why
Three windows per kit Separate return probabilities for days 0–14, days 15–90 and after day 90 Targets the reminder effect where reminders could act (reviewer point 4)
Patient random effects Each patient has their own tendency to return promptly (window 1) and later (windows 2–3); the two are allowed to correlate Accounts for repeated kits from the same patient (reviewer point 1)
Time adjustment Post-2022 indicator, linear calendar trend, COVID period, Oct–Dec season Keeps secular trends, COVID recovery and seasonality from being credited to reminders
Patient characteristics Age at each kit, sex, household size, relationship, employment, race/ethnicity, language, text consent, first vs. repeat kit Adjusts for differences between the pre and post cohorts (reviewer point 2)
Subgroup reminder effects The reminder effect may differ by sex, race/ethnicity, language, employment, relationship, age and household size Directly tests whether reminders worked better for some groups (reviewer point 5)
Partial pooling Subgroup differences share one learned “shrinkage” scale; small groups are pulled toward the overall effect Prevents small groups from producing extreme, unreliable estimates
Text-consent check Patients who declined texts get their own, unpooled terms for days 15–90 and after day 90 They should show no effect; a built-in placebo
After-reminder window A separate post-period term for returns after day 90 Captures late responses to the final texts without counting them as active reminder time
Effects in percentage points Each post-period kit’s return probability is predicted with the reminder program on and off, then averaged Reports results on the scale clinicians use, not only as odds ratios

3.3 Mathematical Specification

For kit \(i\) from patient \(j\), let \(p_{1i}\), \(p_{2i}\) and \(p_{3i}\) be the probabilities of return in windows 1, 2 and 3, each given the kit was still out at the start of that window. The probability that the kit is ever returned is

\[P(\text{returned}_i) = p_{1i} + (1 - p_{1i})\,p_{2i} + (1 - p_{1i})(1 - p_{2i})\,p_{3i}.\]

\[ \begin{aligned} \text{logit}(p_{1i}) &= \alpha_1 + \mathbf{x}_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta + \beta_{\text{post}}\,\text{post}_i + u_{j1}\\ \text{logit}(p_{2i}) &= \alpha_2 + \mathbf{x}_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta + \beta_{\text{post}}\,\text{post}_i + \beta_{\text{covid,late}}\,\text{covid}_i + \text{post}_i \cdot R_i + u_{j2}\\ \text{logit}(p_{3i}) &= \alpha_3 + \mathbf{x}_i^\top\boldsymbol\beta + \beta_{\text{post}}\,\text{post}_i + \beta_{\text{covid,late}}\,\text{covid}_i + \text{post}_i \cdot C_i + u_{j2}\\[6pt] R_i &= \beta_{\text{remind}} + \delta^{\text{sex}}_{s[i]} + \delta^{\text{race}}_{r[i]} + \delta^{\text{lang}}_{l[i]} + \delta^{\text{emp}}_{e[i]} + \delta^{\text{rel}}_{m[i]} + \gamma_{\text{age}}\,\text{age}_i + \gamma_{\text{fam}}\,\text{fam}_i + \boldsymbol\gamma_{\text{con}}^\top \mathbf{c}_i\\ C_i &= \beta_{\text{carry}} + \boldsymbol\gamma_{\text{carry,con}}^\top \mathbf{c}_i\\[6pt] \delta^{(f)} &\sim \text{Normal}(0, \tau), \quad \textstyle\sum_k \delta^{(f)}_k = 0 \text{ for each factor } f\\ (u_{j1}, u_{j2}) &\sim \text{MVNormal}\big(\mathbf{0},\ \text{diag}(\boldsymbol\sigma_u)\,\boldsymbol\Omega\,\text{diag}(\boldsymbol\sigma_u)\big) \end{aligned} \]

What each term means

Outcome

  • \(p_{1i}, p_{2i}, p_{3i}\): probability that kit \(i\) is returned in window 1, 2 or 3, given it was still out when the window began. \(\text{logit}(p) = \log\big(p/(1-p)\big)\) puts probabilities on the log-odds scale, where effects add up.

Baseline and covariates

  • \(\alpha_1, \alpha_2, \alpha_3\): baseline log-odds of return in each window for a reference kit: a repeat kit, pre-2022, outside COVID and Oct–Dec, from a patient of average age and household size in every reference category (female, not partnered, full-time employed, Hispanic/Latino, Spanish-speaking, consented to texts), with a patient effect of zero.
  • \(\mathbf{x}_i\), \(\boldsymbol\beta\): kit \(i\)’s covariates (age at dispense, household size, first kit, Oct–Dec, COVID period, calendar trend, sex, relationship, employment, race/ethnicity, language, text consent) and their effects. The same \(\boldsymbol\beta\) applies in all three windows.

Timing

  • \(\text{post}_i\): 1 if kit \(i\) was dispensed on or after January 1, 2022 (reminder era), otherwise 0.
  • \(\beta_{\text{post}}\): change in all windows after 2022 that is not due to reminders. It is identified mainly from window 1, where no reminder could act.
  • \(\text{covid}_i\), \(\beta_{\text{covid,late}}\): indicator for kits dispensed March 2020–June 2021, and an extra COVID effect on later returns (windows 2–3), for example from mail delays. The main COVID effect is in \(\boldsymbol\beta\).

Reminder effect

  • \(R_i\): the reminder effect for kit \(i\) on the log-odds scale. It enters only window 2 and is multiplied by \(\text{post}_i\), so it is zero for every pre-2022 kit.
  • \(\beta_{\text{remind}}\): the average reminder effect for patients who consented to texts, averaged across subgroups.
  • \(\delta^{\text{sex}}_{s[i]}, \delta^{\text{race}}_{r[i]}, \delta^{\text{lang}}_{l[i]}, \delta^{\text{emp}}_{e[i]}, \delta^{\text{rel}}_{m[i]}\): how much the reminder effect for the patient’s sex, race/ethnicity, language, employment and relationship group differs from the average. \(s[i]\) means “the sex group of kit \(i\)’s patient”, and similarly for the others. Each set sums to zero.
  • \(\gamma_{\text{age}}, \gamma_{\text{fam}}\): change in the reminder effect per decade of age and per additional household member.
  • \(\mathbf{c}_i\), \(\boldsymbol\gamma_{\text{con}}\): indicators for “declined texts” and “consent unknown”, and how much the reminder effect differs for those patients. These are not shrunk toward the average, so the placebo check is not biased toward finding an effect.
  • \(C_i\): the post-period change for kit \(i\) in window 3, after texts stopped at day 90 (the “carry-over”). Like \(R_i\), it is multiplied by \(\text{post}_i\).
  • \(\beta_{\text{carry}}\): the carry-over for patients who consented to texts.
  • \(\boldsymbol\gamma_{\text{carry,con}}\): how much the carry-over differs for patients who declined texts or whose consent is unknown. Without this term, decliners would be assigned the consenters’ carry-over, and the placebo check would partly measure an assumption rather than the data.

Partial pooling

  • \(\tau\): the shared spread of all subgroup deviations \(\delta\), learned from the data. A small \(\tau\) means subgroups respond similarly and their estimates are pulled toward the average.

Patients

  • \(u_{j1}\): patient \(j\)’s tendency to return kits promptly (window 1), relative to otherwise similar patients.
  • \(u_{j2}\): patient \(j\)’s tendency to return kits later (windows 2–3).
  • \(\boldsymbol\sigma_u\): how much these tendencies vary between patients.
  • \(\boldsymbol\Omega\): the correlation between a patient’s prompt and later tendencies.

Why the sum-to-zero constraint? \(\beta_{\text{remind}}\) and the subgroup deviations are added together. Without a constraint, adding any amount to \(\beta_{\text{remind}}\) and subtracting it from every \(\delta^{\text{sex}}\) gives exactly the same predictions, so neither is identified and \(\beta_{\text{remind}}\) loses its meaning. That was one of the problems with the original model. Forcing each set of deviations to sum to zero pins \(\beta_{\text{remind}}\) to the average across groups, and makes each \(\delta\) a deviation from that average.

3.4 Priors

Priors are weakly informative on the log-odds scale. They rule out implausible values (for example, a single covariate multiplying the odds of return by 1,000) without favouring any particular result. The Prior Predictive Check shows what these priors imply before seeing the data.

Parameter Prior Meaning
Window baselines \(\alpha\) Normal(0, 1.5) Baseline return probabilities anywhere from about 5% to 95%
Covariate effects \(\beta\); \(\beta_{\text{post}}\), \(\beta_{\text{remind}}\), \(\beta_{\text{carry}}\), \(\beta_{\text{covid,late}}\), consent terms \(\gamma_{\text{con}}\), \(\gamma_{\text{carry,con}}\) Normal(0, 1) Odds ratios mostly between 0.14 and 7
Age and household-size moderation \(\gamma\) Normal(0, 0.5) Modest changes in the reminder effect per unit
Subgroup spread \(\tau\) Half-Normal(0, 0.5) Subgroup differences are expected to be small unless the data show otherwise
Patient spread \(\sigma_u\) Half-Normal(0, 2) Allows large differences between patients
Patient correlation \(\Omega\) LKJ(2) Mildly favours moderate correlations

4 Changes from the Original Model

Original (OMED 2025 poster) New model
Unit of analysis Patient × period counts (binomial) Individual kits, followed through three time windows
Repeated kits Not modelled; kits treated as independent Patient random effects, correlated across windows
Patients included Only patients with a post-period kit (1,941 patients) All patients (2,092), including 148 with pre-period kits only
Reminder exposure Every post-period kit treated as exposed Effect estimated only in days 15–90, when texts were sent; returns after day 90 modelled separately
Time trends None Calendar trend, COVID period, season, non-reminder post-2022 change
Age One age per patient Age at each kit’s dispense date
Subgroup effects Random slopes on two-level factors (not identifiable); language effect confounded with baseline differences Sum-to-zero subgroup deviations with one shared, learned shrinkage scale; language main effects included
Placebo check None Separate reminder term for patients who declined texts
Kits with unknown return date n/a Kept; the model averages over the windows
Reported effect Odds-scale change described as a percent improvement Percentage-point change from predicted return rates with reminders on vs. off
Model checks Posterior predictive checks only Prior and posterior predictive checks, prior-vs-posterior comparison, convergence diagnostics
Data Uncleaned extract Audited data (date corrections, duplicates removed, consistent coding)

5 Results

How to read the plots. Bayesian results are distributions, not single numbers. In the interval plots, the dot is the posterior median (the most central estimate). The thick bar is the 50% credible interval and the thin bar is the 95% credible interval. Given the model and the data, there is a 95% probability that the true value lies inside the thin bar. When a thin bar crosses the reference line (0 points, or an odds ratio of 1), the data are consistent with no effect.

5.1 Reminder Effect

  • Among 2022–2023 kits, the reminder program raised the return rate from an estimated 76.5% to 83.7%: a gain of 7.2 points (95% CrI 4.5 to 10.1).
  • On the odds scale, reminders multiplied the odds of a return during days 15–90 by 2.12 (95% CrI 1.46 to 3.21).
  • After texts stopped at day 90, the post-period odds of a very late return were 2.93 (95% CrI 1.89 to 4.60) times higher than before 2022. This could be patients acting on the final texts a little after day 90, or another post-2022 change that affected only very late returns; these data cannot tell the two apart. It is included in the overall reminder effect above. Only 991 of 4,302 kits were still out at day 90, but this term may still account for a meaningful share of the gain. A breakdown of the effect by window is listed under Limitations and Next Steps.
  • Other changes after 2022 had no clear effect: odds ratio 1.01 (95% CrI 0.76 to 1.34). Once time trends, COVID and season are accounted for, the rise in returns is attributed to the reminders rather than to a general improvement.

5.2 Text-Consent Placebo Check

Patients who declined text messages should not have received reminders, so their true reminder effect should be zero. The model does not force this. Their post-period kits pass through windows 2 and 3 like every other kit:

  • In days 15–90, their effect is \(R_i = \beta_{\text{remind}} + (\text{subgroup terms}) + \gamma_{\text{con,No}}\).
  • After day 90, it is \(C_i = \beta_{\text{carry}} + \gamma_{\text{carry,con,No}}\).

The two consent terms are estimated freely and are not pulled toward the other groups. If the decliners’ returns had risen as much as the consenters’, both terms would be near zero. On the log-odds scale:

  • Days 15–90: the decliners’ effect is \(\beta_{\text{remind}} + \gamma_{\text{con,No}}\) = -0.03 (95% CrI -0.89 to 0.82), versus \(\beta_{\text{remind}}\) = 0.75 (95% CrI 0.38 to 1.17) for consenters.
  • After day 90: the decliners’ carry-over is \(\beta_{\text{carry}} + \gamma_{\text{carry,con,No}}\) = 0.36 (95% CrI -0.83 to 1.48), versus \(\beta_{\text{carry}}\) = 1.07 (95% CrI 0.64 to 1.53) for consenters.

On the probability scale, the decliners’ estimated gain is 0.7 points (95% CrI -5.0 to 6.4), compared with 7.6 points (95% CrI 4.8 to 10.4) for patients who consented. The probability that consenters gained more is 99%. This group is small (117 post-period kits, few of them still out at day 90), so the intervals are wide.

Author note: confirm with the clinic that patients who declined texts received no reminders by any other route.

5.3 Reminder Effects by Subgroup

What this plot shows. Each row is the total reminder effect for kits in that subgroup, in percentage points: the model’s predicted return rate with reminders minus without, averaged over the subgroup’s 2022–2023 kits. It combines the average effect (\(\beta_{\text{remind}}\)), that group’s deviation (its \(\delta\), i.e. the reminder × subgroup interaction), and the other characteristics of the patients in that group. The interaction terms themselves, on the log-odds scale, are in the appendix (Subgroup Deviations). Because reminders act only in window 2 of post-period kits, each \(\delta\) is effectively a three-way interaction: post-2022 × days 15–90 × subgroup.

  • Sex. Women gained 8.2 points (95% CrI 5.3 to 11.3) and men 6.0 points (95% CrI 3.1 to 9.1). The probability that women benefited more is 98%.
  • Age. The reminder effect changes by 0.20 (95% CrI -0.01 to 0.43) on the log-odds scale per additional decade of age. The probability that it grows with age is 97%.
  • Race/ethnicity, language, employment and relationship. The estimated differences are small and their intervals overlap the overall effect. The model shrinks these subgroups toward the overall estimate unless the data show a clear difference, and here they do not.
  • A note on percentage points. The same relative effect produces a larger percentage-point gain in groups with lower baseline return rates. For example, Polish-speaking patients show a larger gain (9.6 points) than Spanish-speaking patients (6.7 points), but this mostly reflects their lower baseline, not a stronger response to reminders. Patients whose language had no matching text version (“Other”) still gained 10.0 points. The data do not show that language-matched messages drove the effect.

5.4 Other Predictors of Return

These odds ratios describe who returns kits, regardless of reminders. They are adjusted for one another and for each patient’s own tendency to return.

  • Timing. Kits dispensed in October–December were less likely to be returned (odds ratio 0.72 (95% CrI 0.61 to 0.83)), as were kits dispensed during the COVID period (0.77 (95% CrI 0.61 to 0.99)). The Oct–Dec effect holds after adjusting for the calendar trend and patient characteristics. Plausible explanations include holiday disruption and travel, winter mail delays, and year-end outreach pushes that reach less-engaged patients. These data cannot distinguish between them.
  • Age. Older patients were more likely to return kits: odds ratio 1.27 (95% CrI 1.13 to 1.43) per decade.
  • Relationship. Partnered patients were more likely to return kits: 1.24 (95% CrI 1.03 to 1.51).
  • Sex. Sex was not clearly associated with the baseline return rate (0.99 (95% CrI 0.82 to 1.19) for men). Differences by sex in the response to reminders are shown in Reminder Effects by Subgroup.
  • Race/ethnicity and language intervals are wide because most groups are small; none is clearly different from the reference group.
  • These are conditional (patient-specific) odds ratios. They compare kits from patients with the same patient effect. Population-averaged odds ratios, which compare the groups as a whole, are smaller in magnitude because of the large differences between patients described below.

5.5 Patient Random Effects

Each patient has two random effects: a tendency to return kits promptly (window 1) and a tendency to return them later (windows 2–3). A value of 0 means “typical for someone with these characteristics”. Positive values mean more likely to return, negative values less likely, on the log-odds scale.

How large are the differences between patients?

The median odds ratio compares two randomly chosen patients with identical recorded characteristics. For returns after day 14 it is 5.1 (95% CrI 4.0 to 6.7): a typical pair of otherwise identical patients differs roughly 5-fold in their odds of returning a kit. This is larger than any covariate effect in Other Predictors of Return. It is why ignoring repeated kits from the same patient (as a chi-square test or the original model does) understates uncertainty. A patient’s prompt and later tendencies are positively correlated (0.61 (95% CrI 0.46 to 0.75)): prompt returners also tend to be eventual returners, but the two are distinct.

All 2,092 patients

Most intervals are wide and overlap zero, because most patients contributed only one or two kits. The model does not over-interpret thin data: it pulls those patients toward the average (shrinkage) and only moves a patient far from zero when they have a consistent record across several kits.

Selected patients

These six patients were chosen to show the range of patient effects and how the amount of data changes the estimate. Patient identifiers are not shown.

  • A (4 kits, 4 returned (4 by day 14)). Strongly positive: returned every kit, mostly within 14 days.
  • B (6 kits, 0 returned (0 by day 14)). Strongly negative: returned few or none of several kits.
  • C (5 kits, 4 returned (2 by day 14)). Near neutral, with plenty of data: a typical patient, estimated precisely.
  • D (5 kits, 5 returned (0 by day 14)). Needs a nudge: slow to return early, but reliably returns later.
  • E (1 kit, 1 returned (1 by day 14)). One kit, returned by day 14: little information, so the estimate stays near zero (shrinkage).
  • F (1 kit, 0 returned (0 by day 14)). One kit, never returned: also shrunk toward zero, with a wide interval.

Do patient effects absorb demographic effects? Not by design. The demographics are in the model as fixed effects (\(\boldsymbol\beta\)), and the patient effects are centred at zero given those demographics. They capture only the variation left over after age, sex, language and the other characteristics are accounted for. The model does assume that this leftover variation is unrelated to the demographics. If an unmeasured trait (for example, health literacy) differs between language groups, part of it will appear in the language coefficients rather than in the patient effects. The demographic odds ratios are therefore adjusted associations, not causal effects. The reminder effect is protected from this, because it is estimated from changes within windows and periods rather than from comparisons between demographic groups.

6 Model Checking

6.1 Convergence

The model was fitted with Stan (4 chains, 6,000 post-warmup draws in total). Standard diagnostics show no sign of sampling problems:

  • Divergent transitions: 0 (target: 0).
  • R-hat (agreement between chains): maximum 1.005 across 64 parameters (target: below 1.01).
  • Effective sample size: minimum bulk ESS 556, minimum tail ESS 1014 (target: above 400). The lowest value is for rho_u.

Trace plots for key parameters are in the appendix.

Computation time. The 4 chains ran in parallel and took 6.8 minutes in total (per chain: 4.1, 4.3, 5.4, 6.8 minutes, including warmup). The model includes 4,184 patient effects.

6.2 Posterior Predictive Check

The fitted model simulates new datasets from its own estimates. If it describes the data well, the observed values (orange) should fall within the predicted ranges (blue). They do for every statistic checked, including the share of patients who return all or none of their kits. A model without patient effects cannot reproduce this all-or-none pattern.

6.3 Prior Predictive Check

The same model was run with the data switched off, so its predictions come from the priors alone. A good prior allows every plausible result, including the one actually observed, without pushing toward any particular answer.

  • Return rates. Before seeing data, the model considers post-period return rates from 32% to 99% plausible (95% range), and the observed 83.7% falls inside. The prior leans toward high overall return rates (median 80%), because each kit has three windows in which it can be returned; the return rate for any single window (e.g. by day 14) is centred near 50%. The data quickly override this lean.
  • All-or-none patients. The priors already expect many multi-kit patients to return every kit or none, because they allow large patient differences (\(\sigma_u\) up to about 4). The observed share sits inside this range, so the prior is not in conflict with the data.
  • Reminder effect. Before seeing data, the reminder effect is centred on zero, with a 95% range of -10 to +16 points. The prior is neutral: it allows reminders to help, harm or do nothing. After fitting, the effect is concentrated at 7.2 points, so the conclusion comes from the data.

6.4 Prior vs. Posterior

For the reminder effect and the post-2022 change, the posteriors are far narrower than the priors, so the data rather than the prior assumptions determine these results. The subgroup spread τ is informed by the data but stays close to zero, which is why subgroup estimates are pulled toward the overall effect.

7 Limitations and Next Steps

Limitations

  • Observational design. There is no randomised control group. The window comparison and the consent placebo strengthen the causal interpretation, but they rest on the assumption stated in Three-Window Design.
  • Cohort definition. Patients were identified through FIT orders between November 2021 and November 2023. Pre-period kits therefore come only from patients who were still with the clinic in the reminder era.
  • Exposure. Individual text delivery was not recorded. Consenting patients with a post-period kit still out at day 14 are assumed to have received reminders until return or day 90.
  • Small subgroups. Several race/ethnicity and language groups have fewer than 50 patients, so their estimates are uncertain.
  • Shared later-return effect. Windows 2 and 3 share one patient effect, because few kits reach window 3. This assumes a patient’s tendency to return during days 15–90 and after day 90 is the same.

8.3 Stan Code

// =============================================================================
// kit_returns_stage.stan
//
// Three-window (discrete-time) hierarchical logistic model for FIT kit returns.
//
// Reminder schedule (post period, 2022+): a text every 2 weeks from day 14 to
// day 90 after the kit was sent, stopping early if the kit is returned. Each kit
// therefore passes through three windows:
//   Window 1 (days 0-14):  returned by day 14?                 no reminders yet
//   Window 2 (days 15-90): returned, given still out at day 14? reminders active
//   Window 3 (day 91+):    returned, given still out at day 90? reminders stopped
//
//   P(kit returned) = p1 + (1 - p1) p2 + (1 - p1)(1 - p2) p3
//
// The reminder effect R_i enters window 2 of post-period kits. Window 3 gets a
// separate post-period "carry-over" term C_i (late responses to the last texts,
// or a changed pool of kits still out at day 90); like R_i, it has its own
// unshrunk terms for patients who declined texts. Changes after 2022 that are not
// reminders (beta_post) act on all windows and are identified mainly from
// window 1. Identifying assumption: absent reminders, post-2022 changes would
// have shifted returns in every window equally on the log-odds scale.
//
// Patients get correlated random intercepts: one for prompt returns (window 1)
// and one for later returns (windows 2 and 3 share it).
//
// Reminder-effect heterogeneity: sum-to-zero deviations by sex, race/ethnicity,
// language, employment and relationship, all sharing one learned shrinkage
// scale tau; linear moderation by age and family size; unshrunk terms for text
// consent (non-consenting patients presumably got no texts -> placebo check).
//
// prior_only = 1 skips the likelihood, giving draws from the prior (for prior
// predictive checks).
// =============================================================================

functions {
  // Linear predictors for every kit. Columns 1-3 = window 1-3 logits under the
  // regime the kit actually had; column 4 = that kit's reminder effect R_i
  // (window 2); column 5 = its carry-over effect C_i (window 3).
  matrix linear_predictors(vector alpha, vector beta, real beta_post,
                           real beta_covid_late, real beta_remind, real beta_carry,
                           vector d_sex, vector d_race, vector d_lang,
                           vector d_emp, vector d_rel,
                           real gamma_age, real gamma_fam, vector gamma_con,
                           vector gamma_carry_con,
                           matrix u,
                           matrix X, vector post, vector covid, array[] int pat,
                           array[] int sex, array[] int race, array[] int lang,
                           array[] int emp, array[] int rel,
                           vector age_c10, vector family_size_c, matrix C_con) {
    int N = rows(X);
    matrix[N, 5] out;
    vector[N] reff = beta_remind
                     + d_sex[sex] + d_race[race] + d_lang[lang]
                     + d_emp[emp] + d_rel[rel]
                     + gamma_age * age_c10 + gamma_fam * family_size_c
                     + C_con * gamma_con;
    vector[N] carry  = beta_carry + C_con * gamma_carry_con;
    vector[N] shared = X * beta + beta_post * post;
    vector[N] late   = shared + beta_covid_late * covid + u[pat, 2];
    out[, 1] = alpha[1] + shared + u[pat, 1];
    out[, 2] = alpha[2] + late + post .* reff;
    out[, 3] = alpha[3] + late + post .* carry;
    out[, 4] = reff;
    out[, 5] = carry;
    return out;
  }

  // Log-likelihood of one kit's observed outcome
  real kit_ll(int outcome, real e1, real e2, real e3) {
    if (outcome == 1) return log_inv_logit(e1);
    if (outcome == 2) return log1m_inv_logit(e1) + log_inv_logit(e2);
    if (outcome == 3) return log1m_inv_logit(e1) + log1m_inv_logit(e2) + log_inv_logit(e3);
    if (outcome == 4) return log1m_inv_logit(e1) + log1m_inv_logit(e2) + log1m_inv_logit(e3);
    // returned, timing unknown: marginalise over the three windows
    return log_sum_exp({log_inv_logit(e1),
                        log1m_inv_logit(e1) + log_inv_logit(e2),
                        log1m_inv_logit(e1) + log1m_inv_logit(e2) + log_inv_logit(e3)});
  }

  // P(returned in any window)
  real p_return(real e1, real e2, real e3) {
    real p1 = inv_logit(e1);
    real p2 = inv_logit(e2);
    return p1 + (1 - p1) * (p2 + (1 - p2) * inv_logit(e3));
  }
}

data {
  int<lower=1> N;                              // kits
  int<lower=1> J;                              // patients
  array[N] int<lower=1, upper=J> pat;          // patient index
  array[N] int<lower=1, upper=5> outcome;      // 1 = returned day 0-14
                                               // 2 = returned day 15-90
                                               // 3 = returned after day 90
                                               // 4 = not returned
                                               // 5 = returned, date unknown

  vector<lower=0, upper=1>[N] post;            // dispensed on/after 2022-01-01
  vector<lower=0, upper=1>[N] covid;           // dispensed in COVID disruption

  // Covariates shared by all windows (demographics, age, time trend, season)
  int<lower=1> K;
  matrix[N, K] X;
  vector<lower=0>[K] beta_sd;                  // prior SD per column of X

  // Reminder-effect moderators
  int<lower=2> n_sex;  array[N] int<lower=1, upper=n_sex>  sex;
  int<lower=2> n_race; array[N] int<lower=1, upper=n_race> race;
  int<lower=2> n_lang; array[N] int<lower=1, upper=n_lang> lang;
  int<lower=2> n_emp;  array[N] int<lower=1, upper=n_emp>  emp;
  int<lower=2> n_rel;  array[N] int<lower=1, upper=n_rel>  rel;
  vector[N] age_c10;
  vector[N] family_size_c;
  int<lower=0> K_con;
  matrix[N, K_con] C_con;                      // text-consent dummies

  // Reporting groups for subgroup effects (ids unique across all factors)
  int<lower=1> n_fac;
  int<lower=1> n_grp;
  array[N, n_fac] int<lower=1, upper=n_grp> grp;

  int<lower=0, upper=1> save_log_lik;
  int<lower=0, upper=1> prior_only;
}

transformed data {
  // Index sets by outcome type, for a vectorised likelihood
  array[5] int n_out = rep_array(0, 5);
  for (i in 1:N) n_out[outcome[i]] += 1;
  array[n_out[1]] int idx1;
  array[n_out[2]] int idx2;
  array[n_out[3]] int idx3;
  array[n_out[4]] int idx4;
  array[n_out[5]] int idx5;
  {
    array[5] int c = rep_array(1, 5);
    for (i in 1:N) {
      int o = outcome[i];
      if (o == 1) idx1[c[1]] = i;
      else if (o == 2) idx2[c[2]] = i;
      else if (o == 3) idx3[c[3]] = i;
      else if (o == 4) idx4[c[4]] = i;
      else idx5[c[5]] = i;
      c[o] += 1;
    }
  }

  // Post-period kits per reporting group (denominators for subgroup effects)
  real n_post = sum(post);
  vector[n_grp] n_post_grp = rep_vector(0, n_grp);
  for (i in 1:N) {
    if (post[i] == 1) {
      for (f in 1:n_fac) n_post_grp[grp[i, f]] += 1;
    }
  }

  // Kits per patient, for the all-or-none posterior predictive check
  array[J] int n_kits_pat = rep_array(0, J);
  for (i in 1:N) n_kits_pat[pat[i]] += 1;
  int n_multi = 0;
  for (j in 1:J) n_multi += n_kits_pat[j] >= 2;

  // Sum-to-zero vectors: this scale gives each element a marginal SD of 1
  real s_sex  = sqrt(n_sex  / (n_sex  - 1.0));
  real s_race = sqrt(n_race / (n_race - 1.0));
  real s_lang = sqrt(n_lang / (n_lang - 1.0));
  real s_emp  = sqrt(n_emp  / (n_emp  - 1.0));
  real s_rel  = sqrt(n_rel  / (n_rel  - 1.0));
}

parameters {
  vector[3] alpha;                    // window 1 / 2 / 3 baseline log-odds
  vector[K] beta;                     // shared covariate effects
  real beta_post;                     // non-reminder change from 2022 (all windows)
  real beta_covid_late;               // extra COVID effect on later returns (windows 2-3)
  real beta_remind;                   // REMINDER EFFECT (window 2, post), log-odds
  real beta_carry;                    // post-period change in window 3 (after texts stop), consenters

  // Heterogeneity in the reminder effect (non-centred, sum-to-zero)
  real<lower=0> tau;                  // shared shrinkage scale for all factors
  sum_to_zero_vector[n_sex]  z_sex;
  sum_to_zero_vector[n_race] z_race;
  sum_to_zero_vector[n_lang] z_lang;
  sum_to_zero_vector[n_emp]  z_emp;
  sum_to_zero_vector[n_rel]  z_rel;
  real gamma_age;                     // reminder effect change per decade of age
  real gamma_fam;                     // ... per additional household member
  vector[K_con] gamma_con;            // ... for consent = No / Unknown (unshrunk)
  vector[K_con] gamma_carry_con;      // carry-over difference for consent = No / Unknown

  // Patient random intercepts (prompt, later), correlated (non-centred)
  vector<lower=0>[2] sigma_u;
  cholesky_factor_corr[2] L_u;
  matrix[2, J] z_u;
}

transformed parameters {
  vector[n_sex]  d_sex  = tau * z_sex;
  vector[n_race] d_race = tau * z_race;
  vector[n_lang] d_lang = tau * z_lang;
  vector[n_emp]  d_emp  = tau * z_emp;
  vector[n_rel]  d_rel  = tau * z_rel;
}

model {
  // Priors (log-odds scale)
  alpha           ~ normal(0, 1.5);
  beta            ~ normal(0, beta_sd);
  beta_post       ~ normal(0, 1);
  beta_covid_late ~ normal(0, 1);
  beta_remind     ~ normal(0, 1);
  beta_carry      ~ normal(0, 1);

  tau    ~ normal(0, 0.5);            // half-normal: most subgroup deviations small
  z_sex  ~ normal(0, s_sex);
  z_race ~ normal(0, s_race);
  z_lang ~ normal(0, s_lang);
  z_emp  ~ normal(0, s_emp);
  z_rel  ~ normal(0, s_rel);
  gamma_age ~ normal(0, 0.5);
  gamma_fam ~ normal(0, 0.5);
  gamma_con ~ normal(0, 1);
  gamma_carry_con ~ normal(0, 1);

  sigma_u ~ normal(0, 2);             // half-normal
  L_u     ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(2);
  to_vector(z_u) ~ std_normal();

  // Likelihood
  if (!prior_only) {
    matrix[J, 2] u = (diag_pre_multiply(sigma_u, L_u) * z_u)';
    matrix[N, 5] lp = linear_predictors(alpha, beta, beta_post, beta_covid_late,
                                        beta_remind, beta_carry, d_sex, d_race,
                                        d_lang, d_emp, d_rel, gamma_age, gamma_fam,
                                        gamma_con, gamma_carry_con, u, X, post, covid, pat,
                                        sex, race, lang, emp, rel,
                                        age_c10, family_size_c, C_con);
    vector[N] e1 = lp[, 1];
    vector[N] e2 = lp[, 2];
    vector[N] e3 = lp[, 3];

    target += log_inv_logit(e1[idx1]);
    target += log1m_inv_logit(e1[idx2]) + log_inv_logit(e2[idx2]);
    target += log1m_inv_logit(e1[idx3]) + log1m_inv_logit(e2[idx3]) + log_inv_logit(e3[idx3]);
    target += log1m_inv_logit(e1[idx4]) + log1m_inv_logit(e2[idx4]) + log1m_inv_logit(e3[idx4]);
    for (k in 1:n_out[5]) target += kit_ll(5, e1[idx5[k]], e2[idx5[k]], e3[idx5[k]]);
  }
}

generated quantities {
  real or_remind = exp(beta_remind);  // conditional odds ratio, window 2
  real or_carry  = exp(beta_carry);
  real or_post   = exp(beta_post);
  real rho_u     = multiply_lower_tri_self_transpose(L_u)[1, 2];

  // Reminder program effect on the probability scale (g-computation over post
  // kits): each post-period kit's P(returned) with the reminder program vs.
  // with it switched off (window-2 effect and window-3 carry-over removed)
  real p_on_post  = 0;
  real p_off_post = 0;
  real rd_post    = 0;
  vector[n_grp] rd_grp = rep_vector(0, n_grp);

  // Posterior (or prior) predictive checks
  real rep_ret_pre;          // share of kits returned
  real rep_ret_post;
  real rep_w1_pre;           // share returned by day 14
  real rep_w1_post;
  real rep_w2_pre;           // share returned day 15-90 | still out at day 14
  real rep_w2_post;
  real rep_w3_pre;           // share returned after day 90 | still out at day 90
  real rep_w3_post;
  real rep_all_multi;        // share of multi-kit patients returning every kit
  real rep_none_multi;       // ... returning no kit

  vector[save_log_lik ? N : 0] log_lik;

  {
    matrix[J, 2] u = (diag_pre_multiply(sigma_u, L_u) * z_u)';
    matrix[N, 5] lp = linear_predictors(alpha, beta, beta_post, beta_covid_late,
                                        beta_remind, beta_carry, d_sex, d_race,
                                        d_lang, d_emp, d_rel, gamma_age, gamma_fam,
                                        gamma_con, gamma_carry_con, u, X, post, covid, pat,
                                        sex, race, lang, emp, rel,
                                        age_c10, family_size_c, C_con);
    array[J] int ret_pat = rep_array(0, J);
    // [period, statistic]: kits, returned, w1, at risk w2, w2, at risk w3, w3
    array[2, 7] real s = rep_array(0.0, 2, 7);

    for (i in 1:N) {
      int per = post[i] == 1 ? 2 : 1;

      if (post[i] == 1) {
        real e2_off = lp[i, 2] - lp[i, 4];
        real e3_off = lp[i, 3] - lp[i, 5];
        real on  = p_return(lp[i, 1], lp[i, 2], lp[i, 3]);
        real off = p_return(lp[i, 1], e2_off, e3_off);
        p_on_post  += on;
        p_off_post += off;
        for (f in 1:n_fac) rd_grp[grp[i, f]] += on - off;
      }

      // Replicate the kit under the regime it actually had
      int w1 = bernoulli_logit_rng(lp[i, 1]);
      int w2 = w1 ? 0 : bernoulli_logit_rng(lp[i, 2]);
      int w3 = (w1 || w2) ? 0 : bernoulli_logit_rng(lp[i, 3]);
      ret_pat[pat[i]] += w1 + w2 + w3;
      s[per, 1] += 1;
      s[per, 2] += w1 + w2 + w3;
      s[per, 3] += w1;
      s[per, 4] += 1 - w1;
      s[per, 5] += w2;
      s[per, 6] += 1 - w1 - w2;
      s[per, 7] += w3;

      if (save_log_lik) log_lik[i] = kit_ll(outcome[i], lp[i, 1], lp[i, 2], lp[i, 3]);
    }

    p_on_post  /= n_post;
    p_off_post /= n_post;
    rd_post = p_on_post - p_off_post;
    for (g in 1:n_grp) {
      rd_grp[g] = n_post_grp[g] > 0 ? rd_grp[g] / n_post_grp[g] : not_a_number();
    }

    rep_ret_pre  = s[1, 2] / s[1, 1];
    rep_ret_post = s[2, 2] / s[2, 1];
    rep_w1_pre   = s[1, 3] / s[1, 1];
    rep_w1_post  = s[2, 3] / s[2, 1];
    rep_w2_pre   = s[1, 5] / s[1, 4];
    rep_w2_post  = s[2, 5] / s[2, 4];
    rep_w3_pre   = s[1, 6] > 0 ? s[1, 7] / s[1, 6] : not_a_number();
    rep_w3_post  = s[2, 6] > 0 ? s[2, 7] / s[2, 6] : not_a_number();

    {
      real all_ret = 0;
      real none_ret = 0;
      for (j in 1:J) {
        if (n_kits_pat[j] >= 2) {
          all_ret  += ret_pat[j] == n_kits_pat[j];
          none_ret += ret_pat[j] == 0;
        }
      }
      rep_all_multi  = all_ret / n_multi;
      rep_none_multi = none_ret / n_multi;
    }
  }
}
